messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Vignette:
Luisa, a 24-year-old Latina woman who works at a busy warehouse, has been struggling with the aftermath of a terrorist attack that occurred three months ago. Luisa had come to believe that the world is an inherently dangerous place, and she can no longer trust her own body to keep her safe. On the day of the attack, Luisa was working late, restocking shelves when chaos erupted around her. She had been scanning the environment for signs of threat as a new habit but didn't have time to react before explosions rocked the building. The sudden movements of people running and screaming put her immediately on guard, but she felt jumpy and easily startled. Luisa found herself unable to make sense of what was happening; there were parts of the event that she simply could not remember no matter how hard she tried. After the attack, Luisa developed an intense fear of sudden movements by others. She had come to believe that she needed to be on guard all the time and found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day. This constant state of vigilance made her wary of making eye contact with other people, often avoiding it altogether for fear of what might happen if someone caught her gaze. The memory gaps left Luisa feeling fragmented; she knew something traumatic had occurred but could not find words to describe it. When memories did surface, they were accompanied by intense rage, which frightened her the most because she wasn't sure how to manage these feelings safely. Luisa's work environment became a daily trigger. The hustle and bustle of other warehouse workers made her constantly scan her surroundings for signs of threat, and she found herself dissociating more frequently. At times, she would deliberately try to leave her body or blank out to escape the overwhelming sensations. Over time, Luisa’s avoidance behaviors started taking a toll on her social life as well. She had grown distant from friends who didn't understand why she couldn’t talk about what happened. Her relationships suffered because of her reluctance to engage with others and share her experiences. This isolation deepened her negative appraisals about the world being dangerous and her body unreliable. Luisa's hypervigilance extended into other areas of her life, making it difficult for her to enjoy activities she once loved. The constant need to monitor her environment left her exhausted and anxious. She found herself on edge even during mundane tasks at work, where sudden movements could trigger a startle response that sent her reeling. What finally brought Luisa to seek help was the realization that these symptoms were not just passing but were significantly interfering with her daily life. The rage she felt when recalling the event left her feeling isolated and alone. She was most afraid of losing control, unable to live a normal life without being constantly on guard. Luisa is hopeful for a future where she can regain some sense of trust in herself and the world around her. She hopes therapy will help her find ways to manage her symptoms and reconnect with others without feeling overwhelmed by fear and uncertainty.
